t: Why You Should Observe Your Students More https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/12/15/why-you-should-observe-your-students-more/
q: But the truth is, going overboard in helping students doesn’t make you a good teacher. In fact, it’s a sign of trouble.
Most misbehavior happens when your back is turned, when you’re talking, or when you’re otherwise busy and distracted with other things.
If you’re in the habit of helping students immediately following lessons, then you’re training them to be dependant on you.
Immediate, focused, and independent practice of whatever you teach your students is critical to their success and associated with better learning and faster progress.
Observation entails an undivided focus on your students—always standing and typically at a distance that allows you to watch your entire class.
Independent work means not dependent on you. And frequent periods of it—silent, focused, and uninterrupted—isn’t too much to ask of any group of students.
x: Linsin challenges the assumption that constant hands-on helping equals good teaching, arguing that most teachers don't observe their students enough.
Quiet, standing observation during independent work reduces misbehavior because most misbehavior happens when a teacher's back is turned or attention is elsewhere.
Observation deepens a teacher's knowledge of students, sharpening lesson planning and pacing.
Quiet, focused observation during independent work instead reduces misbehavior, builds tenacious independence, boosts accomplishment, and gives teachers deeper insight into each student's needs.
Observation deepens a teacher's knowledge of students, sharpening lesson planning and pacing.
Stepping back from constant helping builds tenaciously independent students who ask smarter questions and need less assistance.

q: When meeting with students (friends) who aren’t getting along, it’s important to remind them that as members of your classroom they must treat everyone with respect—best friend and acquaintance alike.
If someone isn’t nice to you, or is untrustworthy and talking behind your back, then you shouldn’t be friends with that person.
The next logical extension of guideline number one is that if they want to remain friends, then they have to apologize, forgive each other immediately, and start being nice.
If one or more students isn’t ready to commit to a renewed friendship, that’s okay. You can’t force students to be friends.
It’s important to note that if you teach these guidelines to your entire class, proactively, you’ll have few if any friendship problems the rest of the year.
Just the important, enduring lesson that friendships are special and sacred . . . And are never to be taken for granted.
x: Students must treat everyone with respect as a class rule, even if they choose not to be friends with someone.

Applied proactively to the whole class, he argues, these principles prevent most friendship conflicts from recurring throughout the year.
The guidelines teach students to value and protect genuine friendships rather than take them for granted.

t: 3 Ways You Should Never Praise Students
q: Too many teachers, though, praise not out of genuineness, not out of a pure motive to highlight hard-earned achievement or excellence . . . But out of their own desires.
The student is praised not in response to any valid improvement, success, or accomplishment, but rather in an effort to mollify, satisfy, appease, and otherwise keep in check for as long as possible.
Often called “caught being good,” this too is disingenuous. The teacher isn’t really impressed with David.
The problem with false praise is that it lowers the standard of what is good. It gives students an inflated sense of their own abilities.
A deeply moving poem, then, chiseled and shaped through hours of dedicated work, gets the same reaction from the teacher as does sitting up straight in one’s chair.
It must be genuine and real and come from the stirrings in your heart.
x: Praise given to placate or manage a difficult student's behavior is disingenuous and about the teacher's needs, not the student's achievement.

He identifies three misuses: praising for personal gain to placate a difficult student, praising one student to manipulate the whole group's compliance, and praising out of an obligation to praise constantly regardless…
Linsin distinguishes genuine praise from false praise, warning that praise given for the teacher's own benefit undermines its power.
